TextBlock.TextLine: St. James's Chronicle, Sat. May 22 - Tues. May 25, 1762. [p. 4]
To the Printer of the ST. JAMES's
CHRONICLE.
Mr. BALDWIN.
WITHOUT pretending to be a
Connoisseur, I love Pictures; and with-
out pretending to have Taste, I cannot help
forming an Opinion of what I see before
me. That I have never studied Painting in
the Schools abroad, is an Objection which
I can scarce expect to be made to me by
English Artists, on whose Works I am now
about to send you a few Remarks. PUBLICK
EXHIBITIONS will, undoubtedly, promote
Arts, by encouraging the Professors of them,
and by exciting a Love for them in the Peo-
ple; but this can never be expected, unless
the Pieces exhibited are accurately observed,
and freely criticised. The following Obser-
vations on some Articles in the Catalogue of
Pictures, &c. exhibited at the Great Room
in Spring Gardens, will, perhaps, be conti-
nued by a Critique on most of the rest, if
you think the Subject, and the Manner it is
here treated, agreable to your Readers.
Miss BENWELL.
N. 4. Four Heads in Crayons. - I am glad
to pay my first Compliments to a Lady.
These Crayons are not without Merit, but
too evidently betray the Female Hand, by the
vast Profusion of Ribband and Blond-Lace
bestowed on each Head. The Portrait of
the Queen, who is drawn in a particular
Dress, is not improperly adorned. It is a
very true Likeness of her Majesty; and I
cannot tell what some pretended Connoisseurs
mean by calling it a Caricature.
Mr. BROCKMAR.
5. Four Miniatures. - One of these Minia-
tures is the Queen - a very strong Likeness,
and the Hair more exact than Miss Benwell's.
- Another Miniature, in the same Frame,
seems intended to represent the King, but
is very indiffrent.
Mr. CHAMBERLIN.
9 A Child playing with a Kitten, Whole
Length. - Very middling.
10 A Gentleman reading. Half Length. -
One of the best Portraits in the Room.
Mr. F. COTES.
The Production of Mr. Cotes, both in
Oil and in Crayons, are excellent. Indeed,
we do not much admire the Lady, Half
Length. No. 12. But the Head of a young
Gentleman, No. 16. is particularly excellent.
There is an exquisite Softeness in the Crayons,
done by this Master, worthy the Imitation of
all other Artists.
Mr. DAVY.
24 A Portrait of a Gentleman.
25 Ditto of a Lady. - Very unlike a Gen-
tleman or a Lady. Oh! Dainty DAVY!
Mr. DAWES.
26 Olivia and Malvolio, in Twelfth-Night.
Act 3^rd, Scene 4^th. - Poorly executed, and
wrong even in the Manner of Representation.
Malvolio should be cross-gartered.
[?] A Street Scene. - A Paltry Imitation of
the in[c]ompa[rabl]e Hogarth.
27 Catherine and Petruchio, in the Taming
the Shrew, Act 3^rd, Scene 3^rd. - May serve as a
Companion to his Olivia and Malvolio.
Mr. DOWNES.
28. Mr. Shuter, in the character of Scapin.
- A handsome Likenss
Mr. GAINSBOROUGH.
30 A whole Length of a Gentleman with a
Gun. - A good Portrait, and pleasing Like-
ness of Mr. Poniz. The Dog well done.
Mrs GRACE.
32 A whole Length of a young Lady. - The
least striking of Mrs. Grace's Pieces.
33 A Ballad-Singer.-Very well, and ex-
tremely natural.
34 Her own Portrait.-Easy, and seems to
be like.
35. An old Woman's Head.-The most stri-
king of Mrs. Grace's Pieces. The Productions
of this Lady make no inconsideravle Figure
in the Exhibition.
Mr. HAMILTON.
36 Andromache weeping over the dead Body
of Hector.-A very large Picture, that takes
up almost a whole Side of the Room. The
Figures are mostly borrowed from capital Pic-
tures, and moderately executed.
Mr. HAWCK.
37 Mr. Holland, in the Character of Jachi-
mo, in Cymbeline.-No Resemblance of Chris-
tian, Pagan, or Man! No Likeness of Mr.
Holland in Person, Features, or Complexion.
Mr. HOARE.
38 A Picture, intended to be given to the
Bath Hospital. One of the best Pictures in
the Room,-finely imagined, and admirably
executed,-all the Figure are excellent: The
Steward; the Surgeon; the sickly Looks of
each Patient; and yet the different Appear-
ance of Sickliness in the Man, the Woman,
and the Child; the Scurt, and Blotches on
their Hands; and every minutes Circumstance
in the Picture, down to the Velvet Coat and
the Table, show great Power of Execution,
and the most accurate Observation of Nature.
Mr. HONE
39 Sir John Fielding, Half Length.-Very
well-but why a blind Gentleman with Bocks?
Mr. JAMES.
43 A View of Rosanmond's Pond.-Very
stiff. I do not like his Trees at all.
44 A large Landskip.-Much better than
the other.
Mr. LAMBERT.
It is impossible to speak too warmy in the
Praises of this Artist. I am glad to find, that there
is sufficient Encouragement in this Country for
such Landscape Painters as himself, and the
S[?], not forgetting Mr. Wilson. The
Winter Piece, No 48, and the View of the
same Place in Summer, (No. 49.) are particu-
larly pleasing. But in No. 50, I think the
great Fall of the Tees is not made sufficiently
capital. I have seen that Fall, and from the
Impression it made on me, I conceive that
the Painter has not made it near so grand and
striking an Object as it is in Nature. I
Mr. LEWIS.
54 A Gentleman's Head.-A good Portrait.
Mr. MARLOW.
This Gentleman's Views are not without
Merit.
Chevalier MANINI.
66 Boadicea encouraging the People to make
War against the Romans.
67 Charactacus brought Prisoner before Clau-
dius.
68 The Sun enters Leo.-I am tempted to
imagine, that the Chevalier mistook the Na-
ture of this Exhibition, and send these Pieces
here by Mistake; as the seem intended for
the Use of the Society of Sign Painters in
Bow-street.
Mr. MORIER.
71 His Majesty of Horseback.-Stiff.
Mr. MORLAND.
72 His Majesty, in Crayons.-Surly.
(To be continued.)

Public, however, are particularly obliged to
him, or to the Society of Artists, for the
Information in the Catalogue, that, this
River divides the Counties of York and Dur-
ham.
Mr. LAWRENSON.
51 Two Heads.-Most flaring Likenesses.
May they please the Majesties!
Mr. LAWRENSON, jun.
52 A Head.-This one Head is much
better executed than the two Heads. Mr.
Lawrenson, junior, is the elder Brother in the
Arts.
